'''Esther Marley Conwell''' (May 23, 1922 – November 16, 2014) was a pioneering American [[chemist]] and [[physicist]], best known for the Conwell-Weisskopf theory that describes how electrons travel through semiconductors, a breakthrough that helped revolutionize modern computing.<ref name="Svitil">{{cite news |last1=Svitil |first1=Kathy |date=1 November 2002 |title=The 50 Most Important Women in Science |url=http://discovermagazine.com/2002/nov/feat50/ |access-date=21 December 2014 |publisher=Discover}}</ref><ref name="Freile">{{cite news |last1=Freile |first1=Victoria |date=18 November 2014 |title=UR Professor Esther Conwell remembered as a trailblazer |publisher=Democrat & Chronicle |url=http://www.democratandchronicle.com/story/news/2014/11/17/woman-struck-brighton-dies-injuries/19170219/ |access-date=21 December 2014}}</ref><ref name="Iglinski">{{cite web |last1=Iglinski |first1=Peter |date=2014-11-17 |title=Esther Conwell, pioneering professor of chemistry, dies at 92 |url=http://www.rochester.edu/newscenter/esther-conwell-pioneering-professor-of-chemistry-dies-at-92/ |access-date=12 April 2017}}</ref> Her work enabled the microelectronics industry, long-distance communications networks, advanced photocopying, solar cells, and light-emitting diodes.<ref name=Rosengren>{{cite book |last= Rosengren|first= Paul Lief|date= 2024|title= Famous Women Engineers in History - Book 6: Esther Conwell|location= |publisher= IEEE-USA}}</ref>

Conwell studied properties of [[semiconductors]] and [[Conductive polymer|organic conductors]], especially [[electron transport]]. In 1990, she became an adjunct professor at the [[University of Rochester]] while still working at Xerox. In 1998, she joined the University of Rochester faculty full-time as a professor of [[chemistry]], focused on the flow of electrons through [[DNA]].<ref name="Iglinski" />

Conwell held four [[patent]]s and published more than 270 papers and multiple textbooks over the course of her career. Her textbook, ''High Field Transport in Semiconductors,'' became the authoritative text in the field.<ref name="Byers">{{cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=CQeKFG01s-oC&pg=PA317|title=Out of the shadows : contributions of twentieth-century women to physics|last1=Byers|first1=Nina|last2=Williams|first2=Gary|date=August 17, 2006|publisher=Cambridge University Press|isbn=978-0521821971|pages=317|access-date=27 September 2018}}</ref><ref name="ETC" /> She received numerous honors, including the [[National Medal of Science]] in 2009.

==Early life and education==
Esther Marley Conwell grew up in New York City, the oldest of three daughters of immigrant parents. Education was important in her family. Conwell took biology and physics, but not chemistry, in high school.<ref name=Ashrafi>{{cite interview |last= Conwell|first= Esther |date= January 22, 2007|title= Interview of Esther Conwell |interviewer-last= Ashrafi |interviewer-first= Babak |location= Niels Bohr Library & Archives|publisher= American Institute of Physics}}</ref><ref name=UCLA>{{cite web |last1= Braunstein|first1= Rubin|last2= Stahl|first2= Frieda|date= 1997|title= Esther Marly Conwell|url= http://cwp.library.ucla.edu/Phase2/Conwell,_Esther_Marly@841873837.html|website= CWP at UCLA|access-date= January 19, 2025}}</ref><ref>{{cite book |last1= Howes|first1= Ruth H. |last2= Herzenberg |first2=Caroline L.|date= 2015|title= After the War: Women in Physics in the United States|location= SanRafael, California|publisher= Morgan & Claypool Publishers |isbn= 9781681741581}}</ref><ref name=SWE>{{cite document |title= Society of Women Engineers Records|location= (LR001539), Box 187, Folder 38|publisher= Walter P. Reuther Library, Archives of Labor and Urban Affairs, Wayne State University}}</ref> Her attraction to the innate order of physics, and her distaste for lab work, eventually led her to theoretical physics.<ref name=":0">{{Cite web |last=Benson |first=Duane |year=2024 |orig-date=March 08 |title=Celebrating Semiconductor Pioneer Dr. Esther M. Conwell |url=https://www.allaboutcircuits.com/news/celebrating-semiconductor-pioneer-dr-esther-m-conwell/ |access-date=November 23, 2025 |publisher=All About CIRCUITS}}</ref> 

Conwell obtained a physics B.A. from [[Brooklyn College]] in 1942, [[Phi Beta Kappa]]. A professor there, Professor Kurrelmeyer, suggested that she apply to graduate school. She attended the [[University of Rochester]] and completed a M.S. in physics in 1945 with [[Victor Weisskopf]]. Conwell collaborated with [[Karl Lark-Horovitz]] and [[Vivian Annabelle Johnson|Vivian Johnson]] at [[Purdue University]] on electron scattering by impurities in [[germanium]]. Her masters was initially classified then finally declassified in 1945 and subsequently her M.S. was awarded in which she determined the Conwell-Weisskopf theory.<ref name="Colburn"/> This theory is one of the fundamental properties for semiconductor physics and a prerequisite for modern electronics.<ref name=Ashrafi /><ref name=UCLA /><ref name=Krauss>{{cite web |date=2015 |last= Krauss|first= Todd|title= Class Notes: Tribute – Esther Conwell '44 (MS): Lived and Breathed Science |url= https://www.rochester.edu/pr/Review/V77N3/0704_conwell.html|publisher= University of Rochester|access-date= January 18, 2025}}</ref><ref name=Polina>{{cite web |last= Polina |first= Ch.|date= November 4, 2022|title= Esther M. Conwell – the woman whose research helped pave the way for the technological revolution|url= https://medium.com/mycelium-network-media/esther-m-conwell-the-woman-whose-research-changed-the-face-of-modern-computing-7ed7c5cddad1|publisher= Medium|access-date=}}</ref>

==Career==
After her first year of graduate school, Conwell was employed by [[Western Electric]] as an assistant engineer*.<ref name=Iglinski />

Conwell received her physics Ph.D. from the [[University of Chicago]] under the advisement of Nobel Laureate [[Subrahmanyan Chandrasekhar]] at [[Yerkes Observatory]]. She was  a teaching assistant at Chicago and graded the work of Nobel Laureates such as [[Chen-Ning Yang]] and [[Owen Chamberlain]].<ref name=Ashrafi />
She was an instructor in physics at Brooklyn College (1946–1951). She returned to Chicago for her orals and earned her Ph.D. in 1948.

She took a leave of absence from Brooklyn College and worked for a year as a researcher at [[Bell Laboratories]] (1951–1952) where she worked with [[William Shockley]]. While there, she became familiar with hot electrons, a field in which she would work for many years. She wrote a review paper on the properties of transistors which became many people’s introduction to semiconductors. The paper also led to her being an expert on the complexity of electronics and holes in semiconductors.<ref name=Ashrafi /><ref name=Garmire>{{cite web |last= Garmire|first= Elsa|date= 2016|title= Esther M. Conwell 1922-2014|url= https://nap.nationalacademies.org/read/23394/chapter/13|location= Memorial Tributes of the National Academy of Engineering (Volume 20) |publisher= National Academy of Engineering|access-date=January 18, 2025}}</ref>

She then became a staff member at [[Sylvania Electric Products|Sylvania]] where she would work for 20 years. Her research focused on semiconductors – theoretical analysis of [[germanium]] and [[silicon]]. Conwell served as a Visiting Professor for the 1962-1963 academic year in [[Paris, France]] at the [[École Normale Supérieure]]. Her 1967 book, ''High Field Transport in Semiconductors'', became a basic text in the field.<ref name=Ashrafi /><ref name=Garmire /><ref name=Polina /><ref name=SWE />  After [[GTE]] bought [[Sylvania Electric Products|Sylvania]], her research focus changed to support of telecommunications and then moved into integrated optics. When [[GTE]] closed her lab, she spent a semester as the Abby Rockefeller Mauzé Professor at [[MIT]], courtesy of her former intern, [[Millie Dresselhaus]].<ref name=Ashrafi /><ref name=Garmire />

In 1972 she joined the [[Xerox]] Wilson Research Center, where her focus changed to glassy one-dimensional materials. She worked with conducting polymers that radiated light when they were properly stimulated. Xerography requires a significant amount of physics – to get an image on the surface of a photoconductor and then transport it somewhere else and Conwell was involved with the transport mechanism. Her research impacted the printers and cell phones that we currently use. Conwell was a research fellow at [[Xerox]] from 1981 to 1998.<ref name=Ashrafi /><ref name=UCLA /><ref name=Garmire />

In 1989, Conwell helped bring the [[National Science Foundation|NSF]] Center for Photoinduced Charge Transfer to the [[University of Rochester]] which was a collaborative effort between [[Xerox]], [[Eastman Kodak]], and the [[University of Rochester]]. She became the Associate Director starting in 1991.<ref name=Ashrafi /><ref name=UCLA /><ref name=Garmire /><ref name=Rosengren />

After Conwell retired from [[Xerox]], she maintained her affiliation with the [[University of Rochester]], where she held a dual appointment in the chemistry and physics departments. She continued to serve as Associate Director of the Center. Conwell worked at the [[University of Rochester]] until her death at the age of 92. Her later research projects led to more knowledge of how electrical charges move through DNA.<ref name=Ashrafi /><ref name=Garmire />

==Awards, honors and affiliations==
Conwell performed extensive professional service and served on numerous government advisory boards. She was active in the [[American Physical Society]], the [[American Institute of Physics]], and the [[Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers]]. She served on the [[Defense Science Board]], committees of the [[National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine|National Research Council]], and the National Materials Advisory Board on Critical Materials.<ref name="SWE" />

Conwell was made a fellow of the [[IEEE]] in 1980 “for contributions to semiconductor theory, particularly transport in both low and high electric fields.”<ref name="Colburn">{{cite journal |last1=Colburn |first1=Robert |title=How Four Pioneering Women in Technology Got Their Big Break |journal=The Institute|date=16 June 2017 |url=http://theinstitute.ieee.org/tech-history/technology-history/how-four-pioneering-women-in-technology-got-their-big-break |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170625232437/http://theinstitute.ieee.org/tech-history/technology-history/how-four-pioneering-women-in-technology-got-their-big-break |url-status=dead |archive-date=June 25, 2017 |access-date=27 September 2018}}</ref>
She was also a fellow of the [[American Physical Society]]. 

In 1960 she had received the Achievement Award of the [[Society of Women Engineers]] in "recognition of her significant contributions as a research physicist in the field of solid state research".<ref>{{cite web |title=SWE Awards |url=https://ethw.org/SWE_Awards |website=Engineering and Technology History Wiki |date=20 October 2024 |access-date=22 January 2025}}</ref> 
[[File:Esther Conwell Medal of Science Ceremony.jpg|thumb|Conwell receiving the National Medal of Science from President Barack Obama]]
She was elected to the [[National Academy of Engineering]] (1980), the [[National Academy of Sciences]] (1990) and the [[American Academy of Arts and Sciences]] (1992). She is the only member of the [[University of Rochester]] to achieve this.<ref name="Krauss" /><ref name="Bohr">{{cite web |title=Esther M. Conwell |url=https://history.aip.org/phn/11502007.html |access-date=27 September 2018 |website=Niels Bohr Library & Archives |publisher=American Institute of Physics |archive-date=9 January 2024 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240109164353/https://history.aip.org/phn/11502007.html |url-status=dead }}</ref>

In 1997 she received the IEEE [[Edison Medal|Thomas Alva Edison Medal]] for "fundamental contributions to transport theory in semiconductor and organic conductors, and their application to the semiconductor, electronic copying and printing industries." Other notable awardees include [[Alexander Graham Bell]], [[Vannevar Bush]], and [[Michael Pupin]].<ref name="ETC">{{cite web|title=Esther Conwell|url=http://www.rochester.edu/news/conwell.html|website=University of Rochester|access-date=2017-04-13|archive-date=2024-01-09|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240109164353/http://www.rochester.edu/news/conwell.html|url-status=dead}}</ref><ref name="Rothberg">{{cite journal |last1=Rothberg |first1=Lewis |last2=Duke |first2=Charles B. |last3=Dresselhaus |first3=Mildred |title=Esther Marly Conwell |journal=Physics Today |date=May 2015 |volume=68 |issue=5 |pages=63 |doi=10.1063/PT.3.2791 |bibcode=2015PhT....68e..63R |doi-access=free }}</ref>

In 2009, Conwell received the prestigious [[National Medal of Science]] from President [[Barack Obama]], for "her broad contributions to understanding electron and hole transport in semiconducting materials, which helped to enable commercial applications of semiconductor and organic electronic devices, and for extending her analysis to studying the electronic properties of DNA."<ref name="medalofscience">{{cite news |title=Remarks by the President in Presenting National Medals of Science and National Medals of Technology and Innovation |url=https://obamawhitehouse.archives.gov/the-press-office/2010/11/17/remarks-president-presenting-national-medals-science-and-national-medals |access-date=21 December 2014 |work=[[whitehouse.gov]] |via=[[NARA|National Archives]]}}</ref><ref name="Rothberg" /> She was nominated by [[Mildred Dresselhaus]], a professor of physics and electrical engineering at [[MIT]] and a [[National Medal of Science]] winner.<ref>{{cite web |title=University of Rochester's Esther Conwell, a Pioneering Woman Scientist, to Receive the National Medal of Science |url=http://www.rochester.edu/news/show.php?id=3707 |access-date=13 April 2017}}</ref>

Conwell received honorary doctorates from the [[University of Rochester]] and [[Brooklyn College]].<ref name="UCLA" />

''Discover'' magazine (November 2002) listed Conwell as one of the 50 most important women scientists at the time.<ref name="Svitil" /> Her legacy includes receiving the 2004 Dreyfus Senior Faculty Mentor Award for serving as a research mentor to undergraduates, the 2006 [[University of Rochester]] Susan B. Anthony Lifetime Achievement Award for her efforts in advocating and promoting women in science.<ref name="ETC" />, and the 2008 [[ACS Award for Encouraging Women into Careers in the Chemical Sciences]].<ref name="ACS">{{cite web|title=ACS Award for Encouraging Women into Careers in the Chemical Sciences|url=http://www.acs.org/content/acs/en/funding-and-awards/awards/national/bytopic/acs-award-for-encouraging-women-into-careers-in-the-chemical-sciences.html|publisher=American Chemical Society|access-date=21 December 2014}}</ref><ref name="Rothberg" /> 

==Legacy==
Conwell has received numerous awards and honors for her contributions to the field of semiconductor science. She was a pioneer in the field of theoretical physics and frequently the only woman in her classes and engineering workplaces. In 1948, the year Conwell received her Physics Ph.D., only five other women in the United States had received a similar degree (less than 2% of the total Ph.Ds.).<ref name=":0" /><ref name="Garmire" /> 

Conwell persisted through many obstacles women faced who worked in nontraditional careers of the era. After obtaining her B.A. in 1942, she worked a summer job at [[Western Electric]] as an assistant engineer. But because payroll did not have a job title code for her gender, her title was changed to engineers assistant and her pay reduced to fit an existing code.<ref name="Iglinski" /><ref name="Garmire" /> Even with her doctorate degree in hand, she was only able to secure non-tenured positions in academia due to the discriminatory hiring practices of the day.<ref name=":0" /> Thus she pursued industry in her early career.

Conwell persisted and was recognized with the highest engineering honors. She was the second woman to be elected to both the [[National Academy of Engineering]] (1980) and the [[National Academy of Sciences]] (1990). She was the first woman to win the [[IEEE]] Edison Medal (1997), the Institute's oldest medal awarded for a career of meritorious achievement in electrical science, electrical engineering, or the electrical arts.<ref name="Garmire" /><ref name="Rosengren" />

Conwell mentored young women throughout her career. Conwell once said, "My life is the story of women scientists making a place in the world".<ref name=":0" /> She received the Dreyfus Foundation’s Senior Scientist Mentor Program Award (2005), The Susan B. Anthony Award from the [[University of Rochester]] (2006), and the [[American Chemical Society]] Award for Encouraging Women into Careers in the Chemical Sciences (2008).<ref name="Garmire" /><ref name="Rosengren" />

The Esther M. Conwell Graduate Fellowship was established by her son, Lewis Rothberg and his wife, Shelby Nelson. It provides stipends for merit-based fellowships for advanced graduate students pursuing a PhD in Chemistry at the [[University of Rochester]] who show exceptional promise as researchers.<ref>{{cite magazine |date= 2014–2015|title= Department Mourns the Loss of Esther Conwell|url= https://www.sas.rochester.edu/chm/assets/files/newsletter/newsletter15.pdf|magazine= University or Rochester Chemistry Department Newslette|location= |publisher= University of Rochester Chemistry Department|access-date=January 22, 2025}}</ref>

==Personal life==
Conwell married Abraham Rothberg, a novelist, in 1944.<ref name="Garmire" /> Their son, Lewis Rothberg, is also a tenured professor of physics, physical chemistry, and chemical engineering at the [[University of Rochester]];<ref name=Garmire /> his research focuses on [[organic electronics]] and biomolecular sensing using laser energetics.<ref>{{cite web |title=Lewis Rothberg |url=http://www.sas.rochester.edu/chm/people/faculty/rothberg-lewis/index.html |website=University of Rochester |access-date=27 September 2018}}</ref>

On November 16, 2014, Conwell was walking when she was struck by her neighbor's car as he was backing out of his driveway. Capt. David Catholdi of the [[Brighton, Monroe County, New York|Brighton]] Police Department stated that alcohol and speed were not factors in the incident. She was taken to [[Strong Memorial Hospital]], where she died from her injuries several hours later. She was 92 years old and was still actively pursuing research.<ref name=Freile />
